before.overview: Mount Pulitzer (also historically called Snagtooth) is the sixth-highest summit in the Bailey Range, about 0.6 mile from Mount Ferry in the Olympic interior. It is a distinct peak from the separate, higher Wellesley Peak elsewhere in the range, despite the two names sometimes being conflated. The standard line follows the east ridge (the 1961 first-ascent route), typically approached from a high camp near Lone Tree Pass, over heather, snow, and talus. The final scramble to the true summit crosses badly shattered, exposed rock that some parties have judged too loose to finish, opting instead for nearby Mount Ferry. The remote, multi-day Bailey Range approach remains the main challenge.
before.approach: Begins on the High Divide Trail from the Sol Duc Trailhead, leaving maintained trail near the 'Catwalk' below Mount Carrie to join the cross-country Bailey Range traverse. A multi-day approach over rugged, mostly off-trail terrain reaches a high camp (commonly Lone Tree Pass) below Pulitzer and Mount Ferry, from which the east ridge is scrambled to the summit.

climbing_route.label: East ridge to the summit
climbing_route.notes: From the high camp (commonly Lone Tree Pass) below Pulitzer and Mount Ferry, the east ridge is scrambled to the summit.

access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: National Park wilderness regulations; approved bear-resistant food canisters (ARFCs) are required parkwide -- bear hangs/wires are not accepted; pack it in/pack it out
access.permit: Wilderness camping permit required for all overnight stays; the Bailey Range is a cross-country zone not shown on the park's online trip-planner map, so permits must be arranged directly with the Wilderness Information Center at (360) 565-3100.
access.closures: As of the Olympic National Park road-conditions page updated August 7, 2026, Sol Duc Road is open to vehicles, but the Elwha-side Whiskey Bend Road remains closed to vehicle traffic (foot/bike only) due to flood damage, with no end date given -- verify current status before planning your exit.

itinerary.cal: As of the last available report (Sept 2024) the Olympic Hot Springs/Whiskey Bend Road was closed indefinitely to vehicles beyond Madison Falls due to Elwha flood/washout damage, adding roughly 5-6 miles of extra biking/walking each way to reach the Whiskey Bend trailhead — check current NPS road-conditions page before planning.

days.note: Start at Whiskey Bend trailhead (or Madison Falls if the road is still washed out) and follow the Elwha River Trail south through old-growth forest and historic homestead sites. This is a long but gentle-grade trail day to bank miles before the terrain gets rougher.

days.note: Continue up the Elwha River Trail past Elkhorn, Hayes River, and Camp Wilder to Chicago Camp, then leave the maintained trail and work up into upper Elwha Basin (the brushy, route-finding terrain locals call "the maze"). Camp gives a shorter summit push the next day.

days.note: Drop the overnight gear at camp and go light. Climb cross-country up and over Dodwell-Rixon Pass, descend into Queets Basin, then ascend the South Slopes to the summit before reversing the entire route back to camp. Mostly Class 2 walking/scrambling with route-finding through brush and moraine.

itinerary.totalNote: A serious 5-day, ~70-mile round-trip wilderness expedition to one of the most remote summits in Washington: two long days of trail approach up the Elwha River to a high camp in upper Elwha Basin, a long cross-country summit push over Dodwell-Rixon Pass into Queets Basin and up the South Slopes, then two days back out.

before.approach: There is no direct trailhead-to-summit trail. Vehicle access to the Elwha Valley has been closed since a May 2021 washout on Olympic Hot Springs Road; you now walk or bike an extra ~7 miles from the Madison Falls parking area (past the washout, then up Whiskey Bend Road) just to reach the Whiskey Bend trailhead. From Whiskey Bend, follow the Elwha River Trail 28.4 miles (with a ford of the Elwha River at Chicago Camp) to Low Divide (3,602 ft), then continue cross-country up into Elwha Basin and over Dodwell-Rixon Pass (4,783 ft) to reach the SE ridge/south side of Mount Queets. Most parties treat this as a multi-day (4+ day round trip) wilderness objective, commonly combined with the Bailey Range Traverse via Queets Basin to the west. The lower third of the SE ridge is mostly 2nd-class scrambling on crumbly rock and heather; where it becomes impassable, drop a few hundred feet to traverse steep, firm scree around 5,300 ft on the east side to bypass a cliff band, then regain the ridge for an easy 2nd-class scramble around its west side before a moderately steep snow slope on the east side leads to the summit. Microspikes and an axe have been used here even in late August.

before.beta: Mount Queets sits at the heart of the Bailey Range in the interior of Olympic National Park. There is no maintained trail to the summit — reaching it requires a multi-day cross-country wilderness approach, commonly combined with nearby Mount Meany and/or a longer Bailey Range or Queets Basin traverse.
